name: Orforglipron

lead: Orforglipron is a once-daily pill from Eli Lilly that activates the GLP-1 receptor without being a peptide, so no injection is needed. People look to it for appetite control and lower body fat, giving a leaner face and body.

It binds the GLP-1 receptor, which regulates appetite and food intake, so you eat less. Phase 2 and 3 trials in adults with obesity reported dose-related weight loss versus placebo over 72 weeks, and it is sold in the US as Foundayo for chronic weight management. Trials measured weight, not appearance.

paras: It is a prescription daily tablet used alongside diet and physical activity. As a pill it is an oral alternative to injectable GLP-1 drugs. Weight loss builds gradually over weeks to months.

Common effects are gastrointestinal. The label carries a boxed warning about thyroid C-cell tumours that applies to the GLP-1 class, and also warns about pancreatitis and kidney injury, and advises stopping in pregnancy. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Fat-loss-focused users look to orforglipron, a once-daily GLP-1 pill, as an oral alternative to injectables for getting leaner. It lowers appetite and intake, and phase 3 trials have measured weight loss rather than appearance.

lead: Orforglipron (LY3502970), marketed as Foundayo, is a once-daily oral, non-peptide small-molecule agonist of the GLP-1 receptor developed by Eli Lilly for obesity and type 2 diabetes.[1][2] Unlike injectable peptide drugs such as semaglutide, it is a small molecule taken by mouth. It is relevant to appearance because the loss of body fat it produces changes waist, face and overall shape, and because a pill removes the injection step for people who want to lose weight.

A phase 2 trial and a phase 3 trial in adults with obesity reported dose-related weight loss versus placebo over 72 weeks.[3][4] The US label states it is indicated, with diet and physical activity, to reduce excess body weight and maintain weight reduction in adults with obesity, or overweight with at least one weight-related condition, and it carries a boxed warning about thyroid C-cell tumours that applies to the GLP-1 class.[5] The FDA announced approval on April 1, 2026.[2]

Chugai Pharmaceutical discovered the molecule and licensed it to Lilly in 2018; Wikipedia describes Lilly's press material as presenting it as a GLP-1 pill that can be taken at any time of day without food or water restrictions.[2]

paras: The US label lists chronic weight management in adults with obesity, or with overweight and at least one weight-related comorbid condition, alongside a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity.[5] It has also been studied in type 2 diabetes.[6][7]

The phase 3 obesity trial randomised adults with obesity without diabetes to 6, 12 or 36 mg or placebo for 72 weeks as an adjunct to diet and activity.[4] Grokipedia reports weight reductions of up to 11.2% with the highest dose versus 2.1% with placebo in the ATTAIN-1 trial, which should be checked against the primary report.[1] In type 2 diabetes, phase 2 and phase 3 trials reported reductions in HbA1c and body weight.[6][7]

Gastrointestinal reactions such as nausea, diarrhoea and vomiting were reported as the most common events, more frequent during dose escalation.[1][3] The US label lists thyroid C-cell tumour risk, acute pancreatitis, severe gastrointestinal reactions, acute kidney injury from volume depletion, hypoglycaemia with certain co-medications, hypersensitivity and diabetic retinopathy complications as warnings. It notes that orforglipron is not pharmacologically active in rodents and did not produce rodent tumours, and that its relevance to humans is uncertain. It advises discontinuation in pregnancy.[5] A meta-analysis has compared the safety of oral small-molecule GLP-1 agonists.[8]

Orforglipron binds and activates the human GLP-1 receptor, a regulator of appetite and caloric intake.[5] A study in Science Translational Medicine described the structural basis of its non-peptide agonism.[9] Grokipedia describes it as a partial agonist biased toward cyclic AMP signalling.[1] Phase 1 studies tested single and multiple ascending doses in healthy participants and in type 2 diabetes.[10][11] Reported pharmacokinetics include oral bioavailability near 79% and CYP3A4 metabolism, from Grokipedia.[1]
Registered phase 3 trials examine orforglipron in obesity with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, peripheral artery disease, and overweight with risk of complications.[12][13][14][15]

Chugai Pharmaceutical discovered orforglipron and licensed it to Eli Lilly in 2018.[2] Phase 1 and phase 2 results were published in 2023, phase 3 results in obesity and early type 2 diabetes in 2025, and the FDA announced approval on April 1, 2026 as a prescription-only drug.[3][4][6][7][10][11][2] Wikipedia reports UK authorisation in August 2026 and a recommendation by the EMA's CHMP in October 2026 for type 2 diabetes and weight management.[2]

Orforglipron belongs to a wave of oral GLP-1 products intended as needle-free alternatives to injectable weight-loss drugs.[8][16] A 2026 T Nation training-log thread mentions it in passing.[17] Prescriptions are required in the US and UK.[5][2]
Phase 1: single- and multiple-ascending-dose studies tested the drug in healthy participants and in people with type 2 diabetes.[10][11]
Phase 2: a phase 2 obesity trial in the New England Journal of Medicine and a phase 2 type 2 diabetes trial reported dose-related reductions in body weight and, in diabetes, HbA1c.[3][6]

Phase 3 obesity: the 72-week trial randomised adults with obesity without diabetes 3:3:3:4 to 6, 12 or 36 mg orforglipron or placebo as an adjunct to healthy diet and physical activity.[4] Grokipedia reports up to 11.2 percent weight loss at the highest dose versus 2.1 percent on placebo in ATTAIN-1; readers should consult the primary report for exact figures.[1]

Phase 3 type 2 diabetes: ACHIEVE-1 randomised participants 1:1:1:1 to 3, 12 or 36 mg or placebo for 40 weeks in early type 2 diabetes.[7] ACHIEVE-3 compared orforglipron with oral semaglutide in a non-inferiority, open-label trial, and ACHIEVE-5 tested it added to titrated insulin glargine.[18][19]

Meta-analyses have pooled small-molecule GLP-1 agonists, including orforglipron and danuglipron, and a systematic review has covered emerging obesity pharmacotherapies.[8][16] Wikipedia reports that 62 to 89 percent of participants in safety and dosing trials had adverse events, mostly gastrointestinal, with GI events in 44 to 70 percent of orforglipron users versus 18 percent on placebo.[2]

timeline.event: Chugai licenses orforglipron to Eli Lilly.[2]
Phase 3 results published in obesity and type 2 diabetes.[4][7]
FDA approval as Foundayo (April 1); UK authorisation (August); CHMP recommendation (October).[2]
